title: The Placenta and the First Hour
learningGoals: Know what happens as the placenta is delivered
Understand why medicine is given to prevent heavy bleeding
Know the benefits of delayed cord clamping
Understand skin-to-skin contact and the first feeding
Recognize heavy bleeding after birth and act quickly

review.notes: Reviewer: delayed cord clamping is stated as 'at least 30 to 60 seconds' per ACOG CO 814; ACNM favors longer. Newborn medications (vitamin K, eye ointment, hepatitis B) are deferred to lesson 5.2. Heavy-bleeding thresholds are kept general; confirm wording against unit teaching.

slides.heading: The Placenta and the First Hour
onScreen: Labor Basics · Lesson 6
About 12 minutes
slides.narration: Welcome to the final lesson of Labor Basics. Your baby is here. But a few important things still happen in the minutes and hours after birth: the placenta is delivered, your care team watches your bleeding, and you and your baby begin getting to know each other. Many people call this the golden hour. Let's walk through it.

visual.description: Dim, peaceful birth room: parent with newborn skin to skin under a blanket, partner sitting close, nurse quietly charting in the background.

slides.heading: Delivering the placenta
onScreen: Your uterus keeps contracting after birth
The placenta separates and comes out, often with a small push
Usually within about half an hour
Your team checks that it's complete
slides.narration: After your baby is born, your uterus keeps contracting, usually more gently. These contractions help the placenta separate from the wall of your uterus. You may feel some cramping and pressure, and your provider may ask for a small push. The placenta usually comes out within about half an hour, and often much sooner. Your team will check that it came out complete, because any pieces left behind can cause bleeding. Many people barely notice this stage, because they're focused on their baby.

visual.description: Simple side view of a uterus after birth, contracting, with the placenta gently separating. Non-graphic, soft colors.

slides.heading: Preventing heavy bleeding
onScreen: Medicine (usually oxytocin) is given right after birth
It helps your uterus contract and limits bleeding
Your nurse will press on your belly to check your uterus
It can be uncomfortable, but it's important
slides.narration: Right after birth, most care teams give a medicine, usually oxytocin, through your IV or as a shot. It helps your uterus contract firmly, which is how your body controls bleeding where the placenta was attached. This is recommended for every birth, because it lowers the risk of heavy bleeding. Over the next hours, your nurse will also press firmly on your belly to check that your uterus is staying firm. That can be uncomfortable, so breathe through it, and know it's an important safety check.

visual.description: Nurse gently placing a hand on a postpartum person's lower belly, both calm, baby on the parent's chest.

slides.heading: Delayed cord clamping
onScreen: Waiting at least 30 to 60 seconds before clamping the cord
Gives your baby extra blood from the placenta
Boosts iron stores for the first months of life
Recommended for healthy term and preterm babies
slides.narration: After birth, the umbilical cord still carries blood from the placenta to your baby. Waiting to clamp it, at least 30 to 60 seconds, lets more of that blood reach your baby. For full-term babies, this boosts iron stores for the first several months of life. For premature babies, the benefits are even bigger. ACOG recommends delayed cord clamping for healthy babies, and it doesn't increase the birthing parent's risk of bleeding. Some midwives wait even longer. If your baby needs immediate help breathing, the team may clamp sooner.

visual.description: Newborn on parent's chest with the cord still attached, a small timer graphic showing 30 to 60 seconds.

question.prompt: What's one main benefit of delayed cord clamping for a full-term baby?
options: It boosts the baby's iron stores for the first months of life
It prevents the need for stitches
question.explanation: Waiting at least 30 to 60 seconds lets extra blood from the placenta reach your baby, which improves iron stores in early infancy.

slides.heading: Skin to skin
onScreen: Baby goes on your bare chest right after birth
Keeps baby warm and calm
Helps your baby settle and stay warm
Often possible after a cesarean, too
slides.narration: If you and your baby are doing well, your baby can be placed directly on your bare chest right after birth, dried off, and covered with a warm blanket. This is called skin-to-skin contact. Your body is the perfect warmer. Skin to skin helps your baby settle and stay warm. It also supports breastfeeding. Ask for at least the first hour without interruption if possible. Many hospitals offer it after a cesarean, too, and partners can do skin to skin as well.

visual.description: Close-up of newborn lying skin to skin on a parent's chest, cheek turned to the side, blanket over both.

slides.heading: The first feeding
onScreen: Many babies are ready to feed within the first hour
Watch for early feeding cues, like turning toward the breast
Your nurse can help with positioning
If you plan to formula feed, skin to skin still matters
slides.narration: Many babies are alert and ready to feed in the first hour after birth. Watch for early feeding cues, like turning toward the breast. If you're breastfeeding, skin to skin makes it easier for your baby to find the breast, and your nurse can help with positioning. There's no need for a perfect first latch. It's a first try for both of you. If you plan to formula feed, skin to skin is still wonderful for bonding and for keeping your baby warm.

visual.description: Newborn on parent's chest turning head toward the breast, mouth open, a nurse's hand offering gentle support.

slides.heading: Your baby's first checks
onScreen: Apgar score at 1 and 5 minutes after birth
Checks breathing, heart rate, color, tone, and reflexes
Can often be done while baby is on your chest
Weighing and newborn medications can usually wait
slides.narration: Your care team will quickly check your baby at one minute and five minutes after birth. This is called the Apgar score. It looks at breathing, heart rate, color, muscle tone, and reflexes, and it tells the team whether your baby needs any extra help adjusting. These checks can often be done while your baby is on your chest. Weighing, measuring, and routine newborn medications can usually wait until after that first hour together. We'll cover those medications in Module 5.

visual.description: Five small icons for the Apgar categories: lungs (breathing), heart (heart rate), color swatch (color), flexed arm (tone), and a sneeze (reflexes).

slides.heading: Your body in the first hour
onScreen: Stitches for a tear, if needed, with numbing medicine
Shaking or chills are common and pass
Cramping as your uterus shrinks
Bleeding, like a heavy period, is expected
slides.narration: While you're holding your baby, your provider will check for any tears and repair them if needed, using numbing medicine. Many people shake or feel chilled after birth. It's a common reaction and passes on its own, so ask for a warm blanket. You'll feel cramping as your uterus starts shrinking back down, and you'll have bleeding, similar to a heavy period. Your nurse will check you often. And if you're hungry and thirsty, ask for food and drink. You've earned it.

visual.description: Postpartum parent wrapped in a warm blanket, sipping juice, baby asleep on their chest, partner offering a snack.

slides.heading: The golden hour
onScreen: Notice how much can happen with baby on your chest
slides.narration: Here's a short look at the first hour after birth.

video.brief: Gentle, non-graphic footage or animation of the first hour: baby placed skin to skin, dried and covered, Apgar check done on the chest, delayed cord clamping with partner cutting the cord, baby rooting and a first feeding attempt, nurse checking the parent's uterus. Soft music and captions only.

slides.heading: Heavy bleeding after birth: tell someone right away
onScreen: Soaking through a pad in an hour or less
Passing large clots
Feeling dizzy, faint, or a racing heart
In the hospital: press your call button now
At home: call 911
slides.narration: Some bleeding after birth is normal. But heavy bleeding is an emergency, and it can happen in the hospital or after you go home. Get help right away if you're soaking through a pad in an hour or less, passing large clots, or feeling dizzy, faint, or like your heart is racing. In the hospital, press your call button and tell your nurse immediately. At home, call 911. Support people, if your partner seems pale, confused, or faint, don't wait. Get help.

question.prompt: Two hours after birth, you've soaked through a large pad in less than an hour and feel lightheaded. What should you do?
options: Wait for the nurse's next routine check
Press your call button and tell your nurse right away
Change the pad and take a nap
question.explanation: Soaking a pad in an hour or less, especially with dizziness, can be a sign of serious bleeding. Get help immediately.

slides.heading: Your first-hour wishes
onScreen: Skin to skin right away, and for how long
Delayed cord clamping, and who cuts the cord
First feeding plans
Photos, quiet time, and when visitors are welcome
slides.narration: Let's capture your wishes for the first hour. Do you want skin to skin right away, and for how long? Delayed cord clamping, and who would like to cut the cord? Your first feeding plans? And what about photos, quiet time, and when visitors are welcome? Save it to your Birth Readiness Brief, and share it with your care team.
slides.prompt: Write your wishes for skin to skin, cord clamping and cutting, first feeding, photos, quiet time, and visitors.

slides.heading: What we covered
onScreen: The placenta usually comes within about half an hour
Medicine after birth helps prevent heavy bleeding
Delayed cord clamping boosts baby's iron
Skin to skin supports warmth, calm, and feeding
Heavy bleeding: get help right away
slides.narration: Let's recap. The placenta usually comes within about half an hour, and medicine given after birth helps prevent heavy bleeding. Delayed cord clamping gives your baby extra blood and iron. Skin to skin keeps your baby warm and calm and supports that first feeding. And if you notice heavy bleeding, get help right away. That completes Labor Basics. Congratulations, you now know the whole journey from first contraction to first cuddle.

reviewQuiz.prompt: Why is medicine like oxytocin usually given right after birth?
options: To help the uterus contract and limit bleeding
reviewQuiz.explanation: Oxytocin helps the uterus contract firmly, which is how the body controls bleeding after the placenta separates.

reviewQuiz.prompt: Which is a benefit of skin-to-skin contact right after birth?
options: It helps keep baby warm and steadies breathing and heart rate
It replaces the need for any newborn checks
reviewQuiz.explanation: Skin to skin keeps babies warm and calm and helps steady breathing, heart rate, and blood sugar, whatever your feeding plan.

reviewQuiz.prompt: Which of these is a warning sign of heavy bleeding after birth?
options: Soaking through a pad in an hour or less
reviewQuiz.explanation: Bleeding like a heavy period is expected, but soaking a pad in an hour or less, large clots, or dizziness mean get help right away.
